errors.english: people desire the women of others, a suffering of desire devoid of shame
errors.why: The shameless people tormented by desire are the subject who covet others' wives; the English attaches 'suffering of desire devoid of shame' to the women/act.

errors.english: Thus, knowing the many faults of attachment to the women of others, and focusing on stability, one should view them with the perception of a sister.
errors.why: This is a four-line verse in which the steadfast/wise one, knowing the faults, should regard her as a sister and turn away; it is run into prose with the following prose sentence and 'brtan pa' is made 'stability'.

note: Ornate kāvya verse rendered as prose; the sense of the lover's fantasy and the hell warning comes through, with a few mis-attached clauses.

errors.english: just as when there is a distinction in the cause of existence
errors.why: ཇི་ལྟར་སྲིད་པ is 'according as it obtains' (yathāsambhavam), glossed below as 'as it exists, in excellence and decline', not 'the cause of existence' (bhava).

note: The materialist-refutation argument (body vs. consciousness, milk example) is followed accurately apart from one idiom.

errors.english: Even so, this does not mean the capacity is hindered.
errors.why: The Tibetan says that case is not one of unhindered capacity, i.e. the capacity has not yet become unobstructed.

fix.find: this does not mean the capacity is hindered
fix.replace: this is not a case of unhindered capacity

errors.english: Since it is possible for a cause to exist without the result, the answer to the claim that "non-perception does not prove the absence of an object" has been thoroughly explained.
errors.why: 'A cause may exist without its effect' is part of the opponent's objection being answered, not the author's premise.

fix.find: Since it is possible for a cause to exist without the result, the answer to the claim that "non-perception does not prove the absence of an object" has been thoroughly explained.
fix.replace: This also answers the objection that "since a cause may exist without its result, non-perception does not prove the absence of an object."

errors.english: who attempt to negate that the All-Knowing One [note: the Buddha] is free from attachment
errors.why: The Mīmāṃsakas deny omniscient beings and passion-free beings (two items), by reasons such as having a body or intellect that are not incompatible with them; the English fuses this into one proposition.

note: Dharmottara-style discussion of non-perception; the argument is roughly traceable but one negation is flipped and an objection is given as the author's premise.

errors.why: The double negative says the determination of the whole arising from memory and recognition is precisely not uncertain.

errors.english: those individual pillars that lack the power to support a roof
errors.why: The stock example is lifting a beam (those individually unable to lift it can do so together), not pillars supporting a roof.

note: The avayavin debate (recognition, memory, water-jar example) is followed in outline, but a key double negation is lost.

errors.english: then the words for the objects of other philosophical views would not engage without a cause
errors.why: The summary verse says words would not apply to the baseless (causeless) objects of other views; 'causeless' qualifies the objects, and the verse is rendered as prose.

note: Sound rendering of the apoha/pradhāna argument with its verses; one verse line is misparsed.

errors.english: the destruction of certain things is not an uncertain destruction
errors.why: The Tibetan concludes that the destruction of some things is also uncertain: they do not necessarily perish.

fix.find: the destruction of certain things is not an uncertain destruction
fix.replace: the destruction of some things is also uncertain; they do not necessarily perish

errors.english: If one asks, "Why is destruction not initiated if that cause is absent?" that is unreasonable.
errors.why: གང་གི་ཕྱིར closes the opponent's argument ('because without it destruction does not start'), which 'that is unreasonable' then rejects; it is not a question.

errors.english: is a inference of a pervading contradiction
errors.why: This is the reason-type 'perception of what is pervaded by a contradictory' (viruddhavyāptopalabdhi).

errors.english: then producing an effect is not valid
errors.why: The Tibetan says there is no pramāṇa (evidence) for destruction producing an effect, not that producing an effect is invalid.

note: Argument on whether destruction needs a separate cause; the dialectic is partly scrambled and the conclusion of one exchange is reversed.

errors.english: because it is secluded and free from other things
errors.why: The Tibetan says existence does not appear because it is NOT isolated from other things (it lacks such isolation).

errors.english: If it is free from dependence and is known, will it not fail to arise even slightly?
errors.why: The objection is that if cognition lacks a support (object), no cognition at all would arise.

note: Dream vs. waking non-deceptiveness passage; the first half is fine, the latter part on cognizing absence is garbled in places.

errors.english: How can the effect be hollow just because the cause is hollow?
errors.why: The question is how the cause (pradhāna) is also hollow because the effect is hollow; the direction of inference is inverted.

fix.find: How can the effect be hollow just because the cause is hollow?
fix.replace: How can the cause also be hollow just because the effect is hollow?

note: Good rendering of the critique of Sāṃkhya pradhāna (with the guṇānāṃ paramaṃ rūpam verse), one inverted question.

errors.english: the thirteen (sanghadisesa) rules requiring an assembly of the community
errors.why: In the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya the Sanskrit term is saṃghāvaśeṣa; sanghadisesa is the Pali form.

errors.english: This mental resolve is the blessing.
errors.why: བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབ here is the Vinaya adhiṣṭhāna 'to resolve/determine' mentally; the monk should make that resolution, not receive a blessing.

fix.find: This mental resolve is the blessing.
fix.replace: He should make this resolution mentally.

note: Clear, accurate account of the five modes of Prātimokṣa recitation and the reciter's and elder's duties, with two Vinaya term slips.
Faithful rendering of the apoha passage; the translator's note on the probably corrupt 'connected' is reasonable.
